opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and one we think about a lot. With autoregressive models, reasoning is tied to generating tokens left to right. The model thinks by writing out a chain of thought one token at a time, and every token costs a full forward pass. So if you want more reasoning, you pay for it linearly in latency. That's why reasoning models today can feel slow: they produce thousands of thinking tokens before giving you an answer.

Diffusion language models work differently. Instead of committing to one token at a time, the model starts from a noisy or masked version of the whole output and refines it over a number of denoising steps. Each step can change many tokens in parallel. So you're not locked into a strict left-to-right order, and you get a different knob for test-time compute: how many refinement steps you run, not just how many tokens you emit.

That has a couple of nice consequences for reasoning. First, speed. You can still do chain-of-thought style reasoning with a model like Mercury 2, but because you're generating and refining many tokens at once, you get through that reasoning much faster. That changes the economics: reasoning becomes something you can afford in latency-sensitive settings like voice agents, coding assistants, or agentic loops with many model calls.

Second, error correction. An autoregressive model that makes a mistake early is stuck with it. Everything afterward is conditioned on that token. A diffusion model can revisit and revise earlier parts of its output as it refines, which is closer to how people work: you sketch a draft, look at the whole thing, and fix what doesn't fit. For tasks with global structure, like code, math, or constraint satisfaction, that's a natural fit.

I'd be careful not to overclaim, though. A lot of the techniques that made autoregressive reasoning work, like RL on verifiable rewards, long chains of thought, and good data, transfer to diffusion models, and we've used many of them. So it's not that diffusion reasons in some completely alien way. It's more that the generation process is more flexible and parallel, so you get much better quality per unit of latency. There are also open research questions about how best to combine the two kinds of compute, token length and denoising steps, and how to do RL efficiently when you don't have the simple left-to-right likelihood factorization.

But the way I see it, reasoning is fundamentally about spending more compute at inference time to get better answers, and diffusion gives you a much more efficient and parallel way to spend that compute. That's why we're excited about it.

r001.rationale: The response says Mercury 2 can do chain-of-thought reasoning and explains that diffusion generates and refines many tokens through denoising steps.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one we think about a lot at Inception. I think the first thing to say is that reasoning, at least the way the field has operationalized it over the last couple of years, is really about test-time compute. You give the model more time to think before it commits to an answer, and you train it so that it uses that time productively. And the question is, what does "more time to think" actually mean for a diffusion model, because the underlying generative process is so different.

In an autoregressive model, thinking is a chain of thought that's literally serialized. Token one, then token two, then token three. If the model realizes partway through that it made a mistake, the only thing it can do is write more tokens, like "wait, actually," and then go back and correct itself in text. It can't edit what it already said. So a lot of the reasoning traces you see from these models are very long, kind of rambling, with these backtracking episodes, and that's partly a reflection of the fact that the architecture gives you no other mechanism to revise.

With a diffusion model like Mercury, the generation process is fundamentally parallel and iterative. You start from a noisy or masked version of the whole output and you refine it over a number of steps. So revision is built in. The model gets to look at the entire draft, including the parts that come later, and update them jointly. It can fix the beginning of an argument based on where the conclusion is heading. That's a very natural fit for things like planning, or for problems where there's a global constraint that has to be satisfied, like code that has to compile or a proof where the last step has to actually follow from the earlier ones.

So the way I think about it, there are really two knobs for scaling reasoning in a diffusion LM. One is the same as in autoregressive models: you can generate longer outputs, intermediate scratch work, chain of thought, and so on. The other is the number of denoising steps. You can decide at inference time to spend more refinement passes on a hard problem and fewer on an easy one. That second knob is something autoregressive models just don't have. It's a different axis of test-time compute, and it's quite adaptive.

Now, I want to be honest about the challenges too. The whole RL-based post-training stack that's made reasoning models work so well was built around the autoregressive likelihood. You need a way to score a trajectory, assign credit, and push the policy toward the good ones. For diffusion models, the likelihood is intractable, so you're working with bounds or with the denoising objective directly, and getting RL to work stably on top of that is a real research problem. We've made a lot of progress on it, but I wouldn't say it's a solved problem the way it is for autoregressive models.

The other thing I'd say is that the speed matters more than people initially appreciate. Reasoning is expensive precisely because you're generating a lot of tokens. If you can generate those tokens five or ten times faster, you're not just saving money, you're changing which problems are even practical to apply reasoning to. Agentic workloads, interactive coding, anything where there's a human waiting on the other end. So in some sense the efficiency story and the reasoning story end up being the same story. You want a model that can think hard when it needs to, and the only way that's viable at scale is if thinking is cheap.

So my view is that diffusion doesn't replace reasoning as we know it, it gives you a richer set of tools to do it with. Parallel generation, native revision, an extra axis of test-time compute. And we're still fairly early in understanding how to exploit all of that.

r001.rationale: The response says a diffusion model like Mercury refines the whole output through denoising steps and identifies reasoning traces and scratch work as outputs that can be generated and refined this way.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate reasoning from the order in which a model generates its answer. In an autoregressive model, you generate one token at a time, and each new token can build on everything that came before it. That gives you a natural way to express a sequence of reasoning steps, but once you’ve generated something, it’s part of the context—you don’t directly revise it.

With diffusion, the computation is organized around iterative refinement. You can start with a tentative solution and progressively improve it, potentially updating multiple parts together. That’s an interesting fit for problems where you want to propose something, check whether the pieces are consistent, and then revise it.

But parallel generation doesn’t mean you eliminate the sequential work that reasoning requires. If one deduction depends on another, that dependency still has to be handled, perhaps across refinement steps. So the question is how effectively you use those steps, and how much computation you need to reach a good answer.

For a model like Mercury 2, I’d frame the comparison in terms of reasoning quality at a given latency or compute budget. Diffusion offers a different way to allocate that computation. Whether it produces better reasoning is something you have to establish empirically, rather than infer from the generation process alone.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate reasoning from the order in which you generate tokens. In an autoregressive model, you produce a sequence from left to right, and that sequence can serve as a kind of scratchpad. Each step builds on what the model has already written. That’s a very useful way to reason, but I don’t think it’s the only way.

With diffusion, you can think of the computation as iterative refinement. You start with a candidate solution and progressively improve it, potentially updating different parts together. In principle, that gives you a different way to allocate computation: you could revisit an early part of an answer in light of something you figured out later, rather than being committed to every token you’ve already generated.

But parallel generation doesn’t mean you can eliminate the sequential dependencies in a hard problem. Some things really do require working through intermediate steps. So the interesting question for models such as Mercury 2 is how to combine parallel updates with enough sequential computation to solve those problems reliably. I’d distinguish the speed of producing an answer from the quality of the reasoning, and evaluate both. The generation mechanism gives you different possibilities; it doesn’t, by itself, guarantee better reasoning.
